Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway

Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
SUMMARY OF ENVIRONMENTAL OUTCOMES
Introduction
14.1.1.1 Section 2 outlines the details and benefits of the Project together with the
consideration of alternatives during the investigation stage, which has taken into
account public concerns and findings of various engineering and environmental
review. The technical assessments in Sections 3 to 12 have demonstrated that all
the statutory requirements in the Study Brief No. ESB-373/2025 under the
Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) and the Technical
Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-TM) have
been complied with.
14.1.1.2 This chapter summarises the key environmental outcomes arising from this
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) study, the approaches that have been
adopted to either avoid or minimise various environmental impacts throughout the
design process, and the associated environmental enhancements and mitigation
measures.
Environmental Benefits and Environmentally Friendly Design
14.2.1.1 The Project can bring the following benefits:
Avoidance of direct impact to ecologically sensitive areas
14.2.1.2 The recommended alignment and its works footprint have been thoroughly
considered, evaluated from alternative alignment options proposed in previous
stage studies (Section 2.6 refers). This process has resulted in the recommended
alignment option, which aims to avoid both direct and indirect potential impacts on
recognised sites of conservation importance and other ecologically sensitive areas,
such as the Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP), the proposed Nam Sang Wai
Wetland Conservation Park and natural watercourses at Ngau Tam Mei. The
locations of piers are also carefully designed to be outside the Ngau Tam Mei
natural watercourses.
Wetland Habitat Enhancement through Integration and Expansion
14.2.1.3 Under the original alignment, an interchange, I/C-03, (with associated site office
and ancillary facilities) was proposed to the west Ngau Tam Mei Water Treatment
Works (NTMWTW), where scattered and fragmented wetland habitats are currently
found. Compared to the original alignment, the recommended alignment has been
refined, with the Interchange I/C-03 relocated to the south of Ngau Tam Mei New
Development Area (NTM NDA). The viaduct level has also been raised as much
as practicable to provide greater clearance allowing natural sunlight to reach the
habitats underneath the viaduct structures. The relocation of Interchange I/C-03 to
the south of NTM NDA will also provide an opportunity to integrate and expand the
wetland habitats to the west of NTMWTW. Furthermore, the mainline will be
constructed as an elevated viaduct with a limited number of piers, spanning over
the wetland habitats to reduce direct ecological impact to this wetland habitats.
Taking advantage of the Project implementation, the area will not only be reinstated,
but the existing fragmented wetland habitats will also be integrated and enhanced
into a connected wetland habitat. The total wetland area will increase from
approximately 3 hectares of fragmented ponds to more than 5 hectares of
integrated wetland habitats through the incorporation of adjacent village / orchard

14.2.1.4 14.2.1.5 14.2.1.6 14.2.1.7 land. With improved design and management, the enhanced wetland habitat will
support higher biodiversity, greater ecological value and increased carrying
capacity. It will also offer a suitable foraging environment for various relevant
species, including waterbirds.
Allowing Wildlife Movement by Adopting Intermittent At‑grade and Viaduct Design
A section of the alignment runs adjacent to the woodland habitat at the edge of the
Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP) near Long Ha. The alignment profile has been
raised as far as practicable, taking into account site constraints such as CLP cables,
pylons and traffic design requirements. The design has been optimised to avoid
encroachment into LTCP while maximising the length of the viaduct section (Ratio
of at-grade, tunnel, and viaduct is 1:1.14:1.95). Each of the at‑grade sections is no
greater than ~350 m so as to avoid creating potential hurdles to wildlife movement.
The space beneath the viaduct sections provides an open corridor to facilitate
wildlife movement to and from LTCP. For the at-grade sections, retaining wall on
the slope would be constructed to avoid wildlife roadkill.
Viaduct Level Arrangement and Carriageway Separation for Enhancing Sunlight
Penetration and Ecological Benefits
The Project includes slip roads crossing the Kam Tin River, where the viaduct level
has been adjusted to provide headroom of about 10~15m and minimise shading
effects on the water body and associated habitats. In the vicinity of NTMWTW, to
accommodate the required clearance from the existing CLP cable, the headroom
beneath the viaduct is approximately 10m for the northbound and ranges from 5m
to 10m for the southbound. The dual carriageways are separated before entering
the tunnel portal. The resulting gap between the carriageways enables natural
sunlight to reach the ground below and is not expected to cause adverse ecological
impacts. Furthermore, the positioning of piers have been refined to avoid
encroachment into natural watercourses. This approach helps to minimize potential
water quality and ecological impact.
Adoption of non-dredged method for construction works at Kam Tin River
The significance of ecological value of Kam Tin River is well recognised. Given the
large span of the viaduct crossing Kam Tin River, the pile /pier support within the
river is inevitable. The construction of viaduct pier/ pile will adopt the non-dredging
method. For example, if bored pile construction is adopted, steel casing could be
adopted to isolate the surrounding riverbed. The material within the steel casing will
be excavated within the casing for placing reinforcement and concrete of the pile.
This minimises the disturbance to the river.
Synergistic Woodland Enhancement near She Leng
A woodland compensation of approximately 17 ha is proposed near She Leng,
which is currently characterised by grassland or shrubland of low or low to moderate
ecological value. The site is also adjacent to proposed woodland compensation
areas under other projects, including Lok Ma Chau Loop, San Tin Technopole (STT)
and Development of the Loop – Eastern Connection Road (ECR). Woodland
compensation at this location will integrate the overall compensatory woodland area
and improve habitat quality and ecological connectivity with adjacent woodland
habitats.

14.2.1.8 Given the hilly terrain to the south of NTM NDA, the road alignment has been
elevated. This adjustment not only minimises the scale of site formation works, but
also takes into account other constraints, such as the clearance requirement for
CLP power cables. Additionally, a larger headroom would provide greater clearance
between the structure and the habitats so as to allow natural sunlight to shine on
the habitats underneath the viaduct structures.
Minimisation of slope cutting through soft ground tunnelling at portals
14.2.1.9 When the alignment passes through Ngau Tam Shan and Hadden Hill, soft ground
tunnelling has been adopted at portals. Specifically, before the tunnel excavation
reaches bedrock, soft soil stratum will be improved with injection grouting around
the tunnel profile. Temporary support such as pipe roofing and steel lattice girder/rib
will be installed during the tunnel excavation by mechanical method. With the
adoption of soft ground tunnelling, the extent of site formation is significantly
reduced, which helps retain a larger area of natural terrain and minimise the
generation of construction and demolition (C&D) materials.
Minimisation of slope cutting through construction of retaining walls and soil nailing
14.2.1.10 For sections where extensive cut slopes would otherwise be required, retaining
walls / soil nails or combination of both may be proposed. This measure aims to
reduce the extent of slope excavation, allow for steeper slope gradients, and
thereby minimise the project’s environmental footprint, as well as acting as a barrier
to prevent wildlife roadkill.
Avoidance of direct impacts on Sites of Archaeological Interest (SAI)
14.2.1.11 Avoid any excavation works which will cause potential disturbance to the soil matrix
within the boundary of Ngau Tam Mei SAI to avoid potential direct impacts on the
SAI.
Adopt Drill and Blast (D&B) method for tunnel construction
14.2.1.12 Adopt Drill and Blast (D&B) method over TBM (Tunnel Boring Machine) method for
tunnel construction to minimize the generation of C&D materials as much as
practicable.
14.2.1.13 Diverting the existing traffic flow between northeast and northwest of the New
Territories, lowering vehicular emissions from idling or congested traffic and
shortening travel times and results in further reducing fuel consumption, alleviating
potential air quality and noise impact during operation phase.

Adoption of Environmentally Friendly Construction Method and Phased Construction
Arrangements
14.3.1.2 To minimize on-site work and its associated environmental impacts, such as
potential air quality and noise impact from construction activities, as well as C&D
waste generation, precast prestressed concrete construction methods will be
generally employed. This approach shall be adopted for the construction of viaducts,
piles/piers, and building works as far as practicable.
14.3.1.3 The precast concrete girder would be manufactured in casting yard offsite and
transported to site for final positioning and stitching. In addition, the phased
construction arrangement would also help to minimise the cumulative
environmental impacts and to avoid intense, simultaneous pollution.
Implementation of trip-ticket system and GPS or equivalent system
14.3.1.4 In order to monitor, document and verify the disposal of C&D materials at landfills
and public fill reception facilities, and to control fly tipping, a trip-ticket system for
disposal of C&D materials would be implemented. Adopting GPS or equivalent
system for tracking and monitoring of all dump trucks for the Project to record their
travel routings and parking locations to prohibit illegal dumping and landfilling of
C&D materials.
Implementation of environmental monitoring and auditing system
14.3.1.5 In addition to the mitigation measures as described above (see more details in the
Implementation Schedule of Recommended Mitigation Measures as given in the
stand-alone EM&A Manual), a comprehensive environmental monitoring and
auditing programme would be implemented to cover various aspects of concerns.
An Environmental Team would be employed to conduct the EM&A programme and
ensure the Contractor’s compliance with the project’s environmental performance
requirements during construction. An Independent Environmental Checker would
also be employed to ensure that all the necessary mitigation measures are
implemented in a timely and orderly manner.
